LIMITED PROTEST OF THE NRG COMPANIES 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (the “Commission”)1 and in accordance with the Commission’s notice 
issued August 3, 2026,2 the NRG Companies3 hereby submit this limited protest to the July 31, 
2026, filing by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”)4 proposing a Reliability Backstop 
Procurement (the “RBP”), a one-time procurement of new capacity to cover shortfalls in the Base 
Residual Auctions for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year (the “2027/2028 BRA”) and 2028/2029 
Delivery Year (the “2028/2029 BRA”).5  The NRG Companies are supportive of the RBP concept 
and are filing this limited protest with respect to two discrete and severable elements of the July 31 
Filing that are not just and reasonable and should be modified.  For the reasons set forth herein and

I. 
 
BACKGROUND 
As indicated in the July 31 Filing, both the 2027/2028 BRA and the 2028/2029 BRA 
cleared at the market price cap of $325/MW-day and over 6 GW short of the applicable PJM 
Regional Reliability Requirement.6  In the July 31 Filing, PJM proposes the RBP to procure 
capacity outside the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) construct to a target based on the shortfall 
in the 2028/2029 BRA for commitment periods of up to 15 years ending, in all cases, with the 
2042/2043 Delivery Year.7  PJM describes the RBP as “a critical safety net designed to address 
current resource adequacy shortfalls”8 and explains that the 15-year term is informed by the 
statement of principles agreed between and among governors of PJM states and the National 
Energy Dominance Council,9 “which seeks ‘[r]evenue [c]ertainty to [n]ew [g]eneration’ through 
‘15-year price certainty for new capacity resources.’”10

The RBP will be a pay-as-bid auction conducted for three weeks following Commission 
acceptance of the July 31 Filing.11  PJM proposes a soft cap, or “maximum willingness to pay,”12 
of $555/MW-day applied to all selected offers on a MW-weighted average basis over all Delivery 
Years of the RBP.13  This figure represents the cap that would have applied under the Variable 
Resource Requirement (“VRR”) curve for the 2028/2029 BRA but for the separate price collar.14   
RBP commitments will be settled as contracts-for-differences with the seller’s offer price 
as the strike price and the RPM Auction clearing price as the market price.15  Subject to a narrow 
exception, a supplier with an RBP commitment is required to submit price-taker offers into RPM 
Auctions for the Delivery Years covered by its RBP commitment.16  PJM states that this 
requirement is meant to ensure that “load does not double pay for capacity.”17 
II. 
 
PROTEST 
As noted, the NRG Companies generally support PJM’s RBP proposal as a necessary “stop-
gap solution[]”18 to fill the reliability gap.  Nonetheless, there are two elements of that proposal 
that are not just and reasonable and that must be modified to ensure that the RBP serves its intended 
purpose and does not create further market distortions that will, in turn, necessitate further one-off 
solutions.  First, the soft cap is set at a level that does not adequately reflect current costs of adding

Second, the price-taker requirement for offers into RPM Auctions from resources with RBP 
commitments should be eliminated, and an offer floor should be imposed if and to the extent that 
the associated load does not materialize in order to prevent systematic price distortion. 
Importantly, the proposed modifications do not present concerns under NRG Power 
Marketing, LLC v. FERC,20 because PJM has “consent[ed] to the Commission’s exercise of 
authority to modify and/or sever any element of the proposed [PJM] Tariff and RAA 
language . . . [,] where such modification and/or severance is consistent with PJM’s overarching 
objectives in this filing.”21  As PJM notes, the July 31 Filing “is not a stakeholder compromise 
package,”22 so these modifications will not upset the terms of a proposal that was “the subject of 
extensive negotiation and compromise among PJM’s stakeholders.”23  And the NRG Companies’ 
proposed modifications, while important, are “minor deviations” from PJM’s proposal,24 that will 
not have the Commission “transform[ing] [PJM’s] proposal into an entirely new rate of FERC’s 
own making.”25

PJM requests that if the Commission requires modifications, it “expressly prescribe the 
revised rate or rule in its order.”26  In keeping with that request, the NRG Companies have proposed 
specific modifications to the RBP proposal that the Commission could expressly prescribe as 
conditions to its acceptance of the July 31 Filing. 
A. 
Any Soft Cap Should Be Set at a Level Reflecting Current Costs of Resources Whose 
Capacity Could Be Procured through the RBP 
PJM fails to carry its burden to demonstrate that setting the RBP soft cap at $555/MW-day 
is just and reasonable.  PJM asserts that its “proposal to limit the maximum willingness to pay is 
necessary,” because “[t]he RBP is not disciplined by direct buy bids that explicitly express 
willingness to pay.”27  According to PJM, “it is not reasonable to assume that load should be 
obligated to pay an unlimited amount for supply.”28  The $555/MW-hour figure was calculated 
based on outdated estimates of the cost of new entry (“CONE”) and the energy and ancillary 
services revenues for the reference combustion turbine (“CT”) in PJM’s most recent quadrennial 
review.  As such, it is not representative of the current CONE for such a unit, much less of the 
costs of other resources whose capacity could be procured through the RBP, including resources 
whose technology or circumstances do not match those of the reference CT. 
As an initial matter, while the NRG Companies understand the “consumer protection 
considerations”29 that have prompted PJM’s decision to impose a cap, it bears emphasis that the 
Commission’s statutory mission under the Federal Power Act is not just to protect consumers from

excessive rates but “to encourage the orderly development of plentiful supplies of electricity . . . at 
reasonable prices.”30  As Dr. Morris observes, running the RBP with any cap necessarily increases 
the risk that the RBP will clear short, because if the cap binds, PJM will not procure the full RBP 
target.31  As he puts it, the assumption implicit in the soft cap proposal is that “it is just and 
reasonable to sacrifice reliability in exchange for lower RBP Prices.”32  With the last two BRAs 
having failed to procure adequate, much less plentiful, supplies of capacity, the NRG Companies 
do not believe such a sacrifice is justified, particularly when, as Dr. Morris notes, “[m]arket power 
is not a concern with the prices in the [RBP].”33  The top priority here should be allowing the RBP 
to fulfill its purpose of covering the shortfall.   
Further, the assumed tradeoff between reliability and cost does not exist.  It is true that the 
cap, if it binds, will sacrifice reliability for lower RBP prices.  But, as Dr. Morris explains, the 
interplay between the RBP and the RPM Auctions is such that, over time, consumers will have 
sacrificed reliability in exchange for higher, not lower, prices overall.34  If the soft cap binds and 
the RBP clears short, there will be less capacity available for future RPM Auctions (or other 
capacity constructs to incent current capacity to stay in the market), which will increase the single 
clearing prices paid to all capacity cleared in those auctions.35  Dr. Morris observes that the 
increased costs resulting from higher clearing prices in those future RPM Auctions – which will

likely to dwarf the added cost of acquiring more capacity through the RBP.36 
Even assuming arguendo that some cap is appropriate, PJM fails to explain why a soft cap 
based on CONE for the reference CT in the last quadrennial review is a just and reasonable level 
for this soft cap.  The best it can offer is that the longer commitment term provides benefits to 
suppliers such that “it is reasonable to conclude that PJM’s willingness to pay for a 15-year 
commitment should not exceed the amount that load would be willing to pay for a single-year 
commitment under the RPM framework for the targeted Delivery Year.”37  But the RBP is not a 
BRA.  A BRA is a single clearing-price auction for a uniform commodity with a downward sloping 
demand curve designed to send price signals “guiding resource entry and exit.”38  In contrast, the 
RBP is a one-time, pay-as-bid auction being conducted solely for the purpose of procuring enough 
new capacity to cover the shortfall from the last two BRAs.39  Indeed, PJM itself highlights the 
distinct nature of the RBP, including the fact that it is “not . . . procuring a uniform commodity”40 
and that it has no “‘marginal unit’ in any meaningful sense of the term . . . .”41   
The NRG Companies do not disagree with the implicit assumption that, all other things 
being equal, a supplier should be willing to accept a lower price for a commitment of up to 15 
years than it would be for the one-year commitment obtained through an RPM Auction.  The

problem is that, as is often the case, all other things are not equal.  There are a number of material 
risks concerning both the costs associated of new construction as well as the risks and costs of 
providing service out 15 Delivery Years, including, but not limited to, indeterminate network 
upgrade costs that may be allocated to a new project, costs and risks associated with uncertainty 
about potential changes in Effective Load Carrying Capability, fuel delivery costs, and energy and 
ancillary services prices.  Indeed, Dr. Morris explains that the $450/MW-day energy and ancillary 
services offset underlying the $555/MW-day soft cap exacerbates the risk surrounding future 
energy and ancillary services prices, as this level is substantially higher than past offsets and the 
average of the offsets over the previous nine BRAs, which would be $225.49/MW-day.42 
There is no logical reason why the prices paid to individual suppliers in the RBP should be 
subject to a cap based on CONE for a CT when the capacity shortfall could be covered with any 
number of resources, including resources using different technologies or having other 
characteristics that cause their costs to significantly exceed those of the reference CT.  None of 
that variation is captured in the price of the reference CT, which is only “a representative, 
theoretical new plant.”43  As the Commission has observed, a “reference unit is hypothetical, and 
the actual new entrant may be different . . . .”44  That the costs of new entry can vary dramatically 
based on technology and location is illustrated by the range of default MOPR Offer Floor Prices

If the Commission is not going to eliminate the soft cap, the NRG Companies would urge 
the Commission to reset it at a level reflecting a more current estimate of the reference CT’s CONE 
and an energy and ancillary services offset that better accounts for the risks around future energy 
and ancillary services prices.  Dr. Morris calculated such a cap price using an updated CONE of 
$900/MW-day51 and the average of the energy and ancillary services offsets for the nine BRAs 
prior to the 2028/2029 BRA ($225/MW-day).52  This calculation yields a soft cap of $866/MW-
day.53  If the RBP is going to be run with a soft cap, the NRG Companies urge that the soft cap be 
reset at $866/MW-day, which will reduce the risk that the RBP clears short. 
B. 
The Commission Should Impose a Price Floor on Offers for Resources with RBP 
Commitments to the Extent the Load Prompting the RBP Does Not Materialize 
As Dr. Morris explains, the proposed requirement that resources with RBP commitments 
offer as price-takers into RPM Auctions for the associated Delivery Years “is antithetical to 
creating a normal capacity market.”54  PJM itself has recognized the “credibility trap” where “[t]he 
signal that is required to attract investment is the same signal that triggers the intervention that 
undermines it.”55  After interventions that produced “unsustainably low price levels for three 
delivery years,”56 Dr. Morris states, “the market is waiting for PJM – and implicitly, the 
Commission – to make credible moves that they will not allow capacity prices to crash to levels 
that make new investments likely unprofitable over the life of the assets.”57  In this environment,

To be clear, a requirement that resources with RBP commitments offer as price-takers is 
not necessary to ensure that load does not pay twice for the same capacity.  Dr. Morris describes 
an alternative approach that would achieve the same result without such a requirement.59  Under 
this approach, commitments would be structured so that any RBP capacity that does not clear in 
an RPM Auction has its strike price reset to zero for that RPM Auction and all future RPM Auctions 
for the remainder of the commitment period.60  The RBP supplier would have a compelling 
incentive to ensure that its capacity clears the RPM Auctions, but it would still be a voluntary 
choice.61 
Even if the price-taker offer requirement is retained, the Commission should direct PJM to 
establish a narrow exception to this requirement that would apply when the forecasted load for 
which PJM is procuring through the RBP does not materialize.  In the July 31 Filing, PJM proposed 
measures to protect load in the event new capacity procured through the RBP does not materialize62 
and to protect cooperatives and municipal utilities “if a particular large load included in the forecast 
were to fail to materialize.”63  What is missing is any comparable measure to preserve the integrity 
of future RPM Auctions if the forecasted large load does not materialize.  The Commission should 
direct PJM to impose an offer floor on RBP resources if and to the extent the forecasted large loads

set at $175/MW-day (UCAP), which was the floor price applied as part of the price collar in the 
RPM Auctions for the 2026/2027, 2027/2028, 2028/2029 and 2029/2030 Delivery Years.64 
As noted above, PJM has proposed that resources with RBP commitments be required to 
submit price-taker offers (i.e., offers priced at $0/MW-day) into RPM Auctions for the Delivery 
Years of their RBP commitments in order to “ensure[] that load does not double pay for capacity.”65  
If the forecasted load for which the RBP is procuring capacity materializes as expected, the price-
taker offer requirement will approximate the outcome in which both the RBP load and RBP supply 
are excluded from future RPM Auctions.  If the large loads do not materialize, however, the price-
taker offer requirement will depress prices in the RPM Auctions, and this “stop-gap solution[]”66 
to the shortfall in two BRAs could be another in a series of interventions that undermine the 
viability of PJM’s capacity market.  To prevent such an outcome, the NRG Companies propose 
that an offer floor of $175/MW-day (UCAP) apply to offers from resources with RBP 
commitments equal to the forecasted load does not materialize, if and to the extent such a situation 
occurs.  While a floor set at each resource’s actual cost, which would likely be higher than 
$175/MW-day, would also be justifiable, the NRG Companies propose using the previously 
accepted $175/MW-day for the sake of simplicity and uniformity.

In accepting $175/MW-day (UCAP) as part of the price collar, the Commission found that 
it “reasonably narrows potential auction outcomes to maintain investor confidence.”67  The 
Commission also agreed with PJM that the price floor “help[ed] to broadly assure investors in 
capacity supply that in cases where PJM finds it appropriate to intervene in its capacity market in 
extraordinary circumstances, those interventions will not be one-sided.”68  That is, the price floor 
makes clear that, “in extraordinary circumstances like these, PJM will not leave investors 
disproportionately exposed to the downside risk of lower market prices and reduced capacity 
revenues.”69  By its terms, the RBP is an extraordinary intervention:  it is a “one-time, 
supplementary mechanism to procure additional supply to meet the resource adequacy needs of 
the PJM Region”70 outside the RPM construct.  With multiple gigawatts of resources being 
awarded commitments of up to 15 years and being required to be offered on a price-taker basis for 
the duration of those commitments, investors will naturally be concerned about the potential 
impact that this intervention will have on clearing prices in future RPM Auctions if the 
“unprecedented addition of large loads . . . in the PJM Region”71 does not actually come to pass 
and need assurance that this “intervention[] will not be one-sided.”72  The proposed offer floor 
would provide such assurance, will have limited applicability (i.e., only in a volume equal to the 
foregone load), and will apply to a quantity no greater than that procured in the RBP.

8. 
As described in greater detail in PJM’s July 31, 2026, filing in this proceeding, the RBP is 
a one-time procurement of new capacity to address shortfalls in PJM’s last two Base 
Residual Auctions (“BRAs”), specifically, the BRAs for the 2027/2028 and the 2028/2029 
Delivery Years.  As proposed, the RBP would procure capacity commitments from new

3 
supply resources for up to 15 Delivery Years ending with the 2042/2043 Delivery Year.  
The aim will be to procure an amount equal to the 6,831.3 MW shortfall in the 2028/2029 
BRA, less qualifying new capacity serving new load and load associated with certain 
cooperatives and municipals that opt out of the RBP. 
9. 
Among other things, PJM has proposed a soft cap, characterized as a “maximum 
willingness to pay,” for the RBP of $555/MW-day (UCAP).  This represents the effective 
cap that would have applied in the 2028/2029 BRA but for the separate price collar.  This 
$555/MW-day cap is soft in the sense that a supplier’s offer can exceed $555/MW-day 
provided the levelized procurement cost of all selected RBP offers, on a MW-weighted 
average basis, does not exceed $555/MW-day. 
10. 
According to PJM, $555/MW-day is the price at “Point 1” on the Variable Resource 
Requirement (“VRR”) curve approved for the 2028/2029 BRA as part of the most recent 
quadrennial review of Reliability Pricing Model auction parameters.1  In the quadrennial 
review proceeding, PJM described its calculation of the Point 1 price as follows:2

II. 
The Soft Cap is Based on an Outdated CONE Value for a CT and Fails Adequately 
to Reflect Costs of Building New Generation in the PJM Region 
12. 
As PJM noted in a May 2026 report, “capital costs have escalated sharply in recent years.”4  
In fact, as PJM explained: 
Installed costs for new natural gas combined cycle plants now regularly 
exceed $2,200 per kilowatt for projects with commercial dates in the late 
2020s and early 2030s, and costs for more distant commercial dates are 
higher still. This represents a substantial increase over the administrative 
cost of new entry (CONE) estimates that PJM uses to calibrate its capacity 
market demand curve . . . .5 
13. 
In a separate affidavit also being submitted in support of NRG’s limited protest, Dr. John 
R. Morris states that even since the CONE study for the most recent quadrennial update 
filing was prepared, costs have continued to escalate the CONE value  and the proposed 
soft cap of $555/MW-day does not reflect the dramatic cost increases in power generation 
equipment.  
14. 
NRG has witnessed these increased costs in its development efforts. A 2025 paper issued 
by GridLab, Energy Futures Group and Halcyon reflects the “significant and persistent 
increase in the capital costs of new gas combustion turbine and combined cycle gas turbine 
power plants in the United States” and that the “trend marks a stark departure from

15. 
$555/MW-day is low relative to the costs NRG is seeing as a generation developer.  At the 
outset, I would note that even if it were not out of date, the $555/MW-day figure would 
only be tied to the costs of a new CT and would not be representative of the costs of projects 
using other technologies or having other characteristics different from those of the 
reference unit.  For example, NRG currently has several projects under development in the 
PJM footprint using technologies other than simple cycle CT’s that are far enough along 
in the development process to offer into the RBP.   
16. 
However, all of NRG’s development projects that qualify for the RBP are significantly 
challenged by the $555/MW-day soft cap.  One of these projects has a capacity in excess 
of 800 MW and a CONE, less expected energy and ancillary services revenues, 
substantially greater than the $555/MW-day soft cap. This is a well-formed project that 
would, among other things, be located in what has historically been an import-constrained 
zone.  But it is hard to justify the time and expense associated with offering it into the RBP, 
notwithstanding the fact that the soft cap allows offers above $555/MW-day.
